issues.description: Experiment 1 participant numbers do not add up. The manuscript states that 45 participants started, 5 were excluded after training, leaving 40. Later it states that the high-confidence exclusion resulted in 23 included participants but only 5 excluded participants. If 40 entered the main experiment and 23 were included, 17—not 5—were excluded. This undermines confidence in the reported sample size and all Experiment 1 analyses.
issues.quote: 45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants ... Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The confidence scale is reported inconsistently in Experiment 1. The figure caption describes a 4-point confidence scale, whereas the procedure describes a 2-point scale. Because all main analyses depend on identifying high-confidence trials, this inconsistency is consequential for interpretation and replication.
issues.quote: Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty). ... After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.description: For Experiments 2–4 the manuscript says participants rated confidence on a 1–4 scale but never specifies which ratings were classified as “high confidence” for the primary analyses. Whether only rating 4, ratings 3–4, or some other rule was used materially affects trial inclusion, error rates, and the interpretation of “memory illusions.”
issues.quote: then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4). ... Error rates in trials where participants indicated high confidence in their response.

issues.subcategory: probe timing conflated with response timing
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly interprets effects as occurring when memory is probed at 500–750 ms, but participants often made the actual letter response only after a later irrelevant display. Thus the dependent report was not necessarily made at the nominal short delay. Early retrocueing may have allowed selective maintenance before final response, so claims about memory reports within 500 ms or 750 ms are overstated.
issues.quote: 3.75 seconds after the offset of the memory display, the second display was presented for 0.25 seconds ... After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options

issues.description: The General Discussion states that Experiment 1 and 2 probed memory at 500 ms, but Experiment 1 used a 0.75 s cue delay and the actual response occurred later. This misstates the timing of a central manipulation.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)

issues.description: The “memory delay” manipulation is actually a retrocue timing manipulation. In short-delay trials, participants can select and maintain only the cued item for several seconds before final response; in long-delay trials, they must maintain the whole array longer before knowing the target. This confounds decay of a fixed memory trace with attentional selection, retrocue benefits, set-size maintenance demands, and retrieval demands.
issues.quote: In two conditions the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display, in the third memory condition, the probe appeared 3 seconds after offset of the memory display.

issues.subcategory: interference condition confounded with cue processing
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the interference display appears simultaneously with the cue in the Short-with-interference condition. This manipulation can impair cue perception, attentional selection, or source monitoring, not merely degrade the stored memory trace. Therefore differences in error rates cannot be cleanly attributed to memory deterioration by interference.
issues.quote: The Short with Interference condition (panel B) was the same as the Short condition, except that now the second letter display appeared together with the cue.

issues.description: The design lacks a condition in which participants report the target while the display is visible or immediately at offset with minimal memory demands. The authors infer that temporal increases rule out perceptual encoding errors, but without a direct perceptual baseline the initial rate of perceptual confusions is unknown.
issues.quote: To rule out that these errors reflect a perceptual error that has directly been encoded into STM, we test whether illusory responses increase over time

issues.subcategory: temporal increase overinterpreted as memory transformation
issues.description: An increase in errors with longer cue delay does not prove that a correctly encoded percept was converted into an illusory memory. It could reflect retrieval uncertainty, decision bias, differential decay of orientation information, response-selection bias, source confusion, or retrocue effects. The manuscript makes stronger causal claims than the design supports.
issues.quote: This effect must be due to processes ongoing in STM: Had these illusory memories been the result of changes in perception, they should have been present at the earlier probe as well.

issues.subcategory: target absent on critical Experiment 1 trials
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the response display sometimes replaced the target with its mirrored counterpart rather than presenting both. On such trials, a participant who remembers the target but fails to use “none of these” has no correct target option available. This makes Experiment 1 “illusory” responses partly a target-absent lure-choice paradigm rather than a direct memory report between target and counterpart.
issues.quote: The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed) ... If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options.

issues.description: Experiment 1 instructed participants to choose “none of these” when the target was absent, but the results report only illusory and other errors. The frequency of correct “none” responses, high-confidence “none” responses, and their distribution across target types are necessary to interpret target-absent critical trials.
issues.quote: They were instructed to select "none of these" if the target letter was not a response option. ... the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: high confidence equated with illusory memory
issues.description: The manuscript treats high-confidence errors as evidence of an “actual” false memory rather than guessing. High confidence, however, can arise from response bias, familiarity, fluency, metacognitive miscalibration, or demand characteristics. Confidence alone does not establish that participants experienced an illusory memory trace.
issues.quote: Therefore, isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.subcategory: invalid comparison between mirrored-counterpart errors and unrelated errors
issues.description: The primary evidence that “illusions occur” compares selection of the mirrored counterpart with selection of unrelated distractors. The mirrored counterpart shares identity, shape, and likely verbal label with the target, whereas unrelated distractors do not. Higher counterpart selection may reflect ordinary similarity-based confusion or partial memory, not an expectation-induced illusion.
issues.quote: hypothesis 1 - do illusions occur in STM? – by determining if participants confused pseudo-letter targets with their real counterpart with high confidence, or the other way around, more often than other high confidence errors (main effect of Error Type).

issues.description: The pseudo-to-real asymmetry is interpreted as evidence that world knowledge drives the effect, but target type is confounded with familiarity, nameability, verbal rehearsal, response fluency, and response preference for real letters. The experiments do not causally manipulate lifelong world knowledge, and the transient expectation manipulation in Experiment 2 failed.
issues.quote: Moreover, high confidence errors occurred mainly for pseudo-to-real letter memories, and much less often for real-to-pseudo-letter memories, indicating that visual similarity is not the primary cause of this memory-bias. Instead ‘world knowledge’ (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.subcategory: response bias dismissed without adequate test
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that participants may simply prefer selecting real letters, but dismiss this explanation informally. Balancing real and pseudo-letter frequencies does not remove inherent response familiarity or fluency differences between real and mirrored letters; a formal signal-detection or multinomial model would be needed to separate memory sensitivity from response bias.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.description: Real and mirrored letters differ in ease of verbal encoding. Participants may encode a pseudo-letter as the corresponding letter name plus a fragile orientation tag; loss of the orientation tag would produce pseudo-to-real reports without requiring predictive reshaping of STM. The authors discuss this possibility but do not control it experimentally, for example via articulatory suppression.
issues.quote: FTT does suggest that pseudo-letters have a verbal (the letter itself) and a gist level (“mirrored”) representation, while real letters can be stored purely at the verbal level. This would mean that verbal rehearsal is more effective to store a complete representation of real letters in working memory, but not for pseudo-letters.

issues.description: The analyses use repeated-measures ANOVA on per-participant error percentages. These outcomes are bounded proportions derived from binomial counts with unequal denominators after conditioning on high confidence. This can violate normality and homoscedasticity assumptions and discard trial-level information. A binomial or multinomial mixed-effects model would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: the relative occurrence of illusory memories (on high confidence trials) was analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), and type of error

issues.subcategory: conditioning on confidence can bias error rates
issues.description: All primary error rates are conditional on trials where participants gave high confidence. If confidence itself varies by target type, delay, accuracy, or participant, conditioning on it can create selection bias and obscure the overall probability of high-confidence false reports. The manuscript does not model confidence and accuracy jointly.
issues.quote: Error rates in trials where participants indicated high confidence in their response.

issues.description: The analyses aggregate over letters and do not include letter identity as a random effect. Mirror confusability, visual complexity, letter frequency, nameability, and resemblance to other symbols differ across letters. Without item-level modeling, effects may be driven by a subset of letter pairs and cannot be generalized over letters.
issues.quote: Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays).

issues.description: The manuscript does not report critical visual stimulus details such as font, letter size, case rendering, stroke width, antialiasing, display resolution, viewing distance for later experiments, or exact letter set used in each experiment. These details are essential because mirror-letter confusability depends strongly on typography and visual angle.
issues.quote: The memory and cue displays were set up in the same way as the displays in the training session, with 6 or 8 letters replacing the tilted bars.

issues.description: Large numbers of participants were excluded because they had too few high-confidence trials, especially in Experiment 2. Excluding low-confidence participants changes the estimand from the full sample to a high-confidence/high-performing subset and may inflate estimates of high-confidence errors. Sensitivity analyses including excluded participants are not reported.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The exclusion rule requiring more than 10 high-confidence trials per cell is central and removes many participants, but the manuscript does not state that this rule was preregistered or chosen before inspecting the data. This creates researcher degrees of freedom because different thresholds could materially alter the results.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less)

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used optional stopping based on a sequential Bayes factor, but the stopping rule lacks key details: exact test specification, prior scale, one- versus two-sided alternative, whether stopping for evidence for the null was allowed, how exclusions interacted with stopping, and whether the rule was preregistered. The stopping statistic also differs from the main ANOVA model.
issues.quote: Sample size was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets. Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

issues.description: The text says non-illusory errors showed a Memory Delay effect with BFincl = 190 and no Target Type effect, but Table 4 reports Memory Delay BFincl = 0.064 and Target Type BFincl = 39110.895. This is a severe inconsistency in the reported statistical results and reverses the interpretation of the follow-up analysis.
issues.quote: Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets ... Memory Delay | 0.087 | 0.913 | 0.064 ... Target Type | 1.000 | 1.705e-5 | 39110.895

issues.subcategory: failed expectation manipulation lacks manipulation check
issues.description: Experiment 2 concludes that transient expectations do not affect illusions, but there is no direct evidence that participants learned or used the color-target contingency. A post-experiment free-response awareness question is not a sufficient manipulation check for implicit learning, and the null effect may reflect manipulation failure rather than absence of transient expectation effects.
issues.quote: The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses. ... However, transiently generated expectations, in this case provided by a cue about the prevalence of real versus pseudo-letters targets, had no effect on the prevalence of illusory memories.

issues.subcategory: cue color confounded with luminance and not counterbalanced
issues.description: In Experiment 2, red and blue cues differed substantially in luminance and were mapped to different pseudo-letter probabilities. The manuscript does not state that color-probability mappings were counterbalanced. Any cue-color effect would therefore be confounded with low-level color/luminance differences; the null is also harder to interpret because the cues may differ in salience.
issues.quote: both the central fixation cross and the cue were either blue (CIE: 0.148, 0.078, luminance: 6.47 cd/m2) or red (CIE: 0.641, 0.341; luminance: 11.9 cd/m2). ... If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on 25% of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on 60% of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue.

issues.description: Experiment 4 used 250 ms visual presentations in an online laptop-based experiment. Precise timing, refresh rate, viewing distance, screen size, luminance, and browser/device performance are uncontrolled or unreported, which is especially problematic for brief visual memory displays and mirror-letter discriminability.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting . Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting ... given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.description: The manuscript reports Bayesian ANOVAs and Bayes factors but does not specify prior distributions, prior scales, model prior probabilities beyond table outputs, or robustness checks. Bayes factors can be sensitive to these choices, so this omission impairs reproducibility and evaluation.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.description: Experiment 1 has no power or sensitivity justification, and Experiment 2 used a convenience sample determined by course enrollment. Given cell exclusions and high-confidence filtering, planned precision for the critical interactions is unclear.
issues.quote: The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course, which explains the large increase in participants compared to Experiment 1.

issues.description: Experiment 1 excluded participants based on performance in a rectangle-orientation change detection task, not the letter-memory task. This may select a nonrepresentative high-performing visual-memory subgroup and limits comparability with Experiments 2–4, which did not use the same training exclusion.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training.

issues.description: Experiment 2 was embedded in a 2-hour session with several unrelated experiments, but the manuscript does not report task order, counterbalancing, breaks, or whether preceding tasks could induce fatigue or influence attention, confidence, or letter expectations.
issues.quote: The experiment was part of a 2-hour session which contained this experiment, and several other unrelated experiments.

issues.description: The manuscript says the increase was “smaller” for mirrored targets when it was numerically larger, indicating an error in the description of the interaction pattern.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.description: The Experiment 4 results refer to Figure 5, but the Experiment 4 figure is labeled Figure 6. This is a reporting error that can confuse readers and complicate interpretation.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. ... Figure 6 Experiment 4.

issues.description: The discussion first claims that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories, then immediately acknowledges that iconic memory was not tested. This is both internally inconsistent and theoretically overbroad.
issues.quote: The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research ... Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from young psychology students and Latin letters
issues.description: The samples are predominantly young university psychology students familiar with the Latin alphabet, and the stimuli are culturally overlearned letters. Broad claims about short-term memory, visual percepts in general, or memory stages across populations and stimulus domains exceed the sampling and stimulus base.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum. ... This implicates that very early illusory memories could be an inherent feature of the cognitive processing sequence for sensory input.

issues.description: The manuscript argues that FTT predicts high similarity should facilitate false memories, then says this is inconsistent with abundant false memories for highly similar mirrored counterparts. That reasoning is logically reversed: abundant false memories for highly similar items would appear consistent with a similarity-facilitation prediction unless the intended claim is about asymmetry, which is not stated clearly.
issues.quote: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories . This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.description: The discussion presents predictive processing as an explanatory framework, but the experiments do not estimate priors and likelihoods, manipulate precision independently, or compare predictive-processing predictions against formal alternatives. The data are compatible with several non-predictive mechanisms, including verbal recoding, loss of orientation tags, familiarity bias, and retrieval decision bias.
issues.quote: Together, these findings suggest that memory of very recent events is promptly shaped by world knowledge, and that the effect of world knowledge increases as time passes and the memory trace itself decays.

issues.description: The manuscript sometimes characterizes mirrored letters as novel stimuli, but they are systematic transformations of familiar letters and often preserve letter identity. Treating them as simply novel versus familiar conflates novelty, orientation, nameability, and category membership.
issues.quote: using a stimulus set that contains the same amount of world knowledge confirming stimuli (real letters) as novel stimuli (pseudo-letters).

issues.description: Participants received trial-by-trial or block feedback emphasizing real versus pseudo-letter accuracy. This may induce strategic changes, response caution, or learning about stimulus distributions across the experiment. The manuscript does not analyze learning over blocks or show that the effects are stable over time.
issues.quote: They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.subcategory: no per-cell trial counts after filtering
issues.description: The manuscript reports average percentages of high-confidence trials but not the actual per-cell denominators used to compute illusion and other-error rates. Because exclusions and binomial precision depend on cell counts, these are needed to evaluate reliability and replicate the analyses.
issues.quote: Included participants had on average 49.2% high confidence trial over all conditions (range: 24.6 – 95.8, sd: 13.3).
